sections.title: Why Docsense is the default
sections.content: Docsense is built so the shortest path to working search is also a complete docs SearchBar: 1. Add docusaurus-plugin-docsense to your config. 2. Run docusaurus start or docusaurus build. 3. Open search from the navbar or with ⌘K / Ctrl+K . You get a deploy-fresh local index, page-type filters, a live page-limit control (3 to 20), typo-tolerant ranking, destination-page highlighting, and documented theming, without standing up another service. Other options remain the right choice when their constraints match your project. They usually take more integration work, a different engine commitment, or a hosted account.

sections.title: What Docsense provides
sections.content: - Build-time index. The plugin writes search-index.json during docusaurus start and docusaurus build, so the index matches the site you deploy. - In-browser queries. Readers search against that static file. There is no Docsense query service. - Documentation-oriented ranking. Titles, sections, code, breadcrumbs, and body text are weighted for docs content. - SearchBar controls. Page-type filters and a Pages − / + control help readers narrow results. The page count cannot go below 3 or above 20 . - Theming and copy. Labels, shortcut, empty-state text, and CSS variables are part of the supported configuration surface. For behavior details, see How Docsense works and Features overview.

sections.title: Docsense
sections.content: Use Docsense as the default when you are building or upgrading search on a Docusaurus documentation site and you want the simplest install-and-run path. It also fits when: - You need an open-source local search path with no search vendor account. - The search index must update with every documentation deploy. - Readers need filters, typo tolerance, and a branded SearchBar. - Private or internal documentation must stay inside your build and static hosting boundary. Next step: Install Docsense.

sections.title: easyops local search
sections.content: Choose easyops local search when: - Your team already runs @easyops-cn/docusaurus-search-local. - lunr-style matching meets your relevance requirements. - You want a widely adopted community plugin and do not need Docsense’s page-type chips or live page-limit control.

sections.title: Orama Docusaurus plugin
sections.content: Choose the Orama plugin when: - You want Orama as the underlying search engine. - You expect to use Orama Cloud or other Orama deployments later. - Category-style filtering and Orama’s relevance model match your information architecture.

sections.title: Pagefind
sections.content: Choose Pagefind when: - The documentation set is large enough that a single up-front index download is a concern. - You index mixed static HTML, not only Docusaurus Markdown and MDX. - You can own the search UI and Docusaurus integration yourself. Docsense currently ships one static JSON index per site. Sharded indexes are listed on the feature roadmap.

sections.title: Algolia DocSearch
sections.content: Choose Algolia DocSearch when: - You want a managed hosted search service. - You need vendor-operated crawling, analytics, or Ask AI. - Your security and procurement process allows an external search account.

sections.title: Current Docsense scope
sections.content: In the current release, Docsense: - Ships a single static JSON index per site - Uses English-first tokenization and stemming - Does not include a built-in Ask AI panel - Targets documentation sites and developer portals Planned work is listed under Feature roadmap.

documents.title: How Docsense works

sections.title: Build time
sections.content: When you run docusaurus start or docusaurus build, the plugin: 1. Scans the docs directories you set in docsDirs (default: docs) 2. Parses each Markdown or MDX file into a structured record (title, sections, body, page type) 3. Writes static/docsense/search-index.json (path is configurable) That file is a normal static asset. Deploy it with the rest of your site.

sections.title: Runtime
sections.content: When a reader opens search: 1. The SearchBar loads the JSON index once (lazy load) 2. Each query runs in memory with tokenization, fuzzy matching, and ranking 3. The modal shows page-level results, optional filters, and the page limit you choose There is no Docsense API server. If the static index file is available, search works.

sections.title: Packages
sections.content: Package Role --- --- @docsense/core Tokenize, rank, and search() @docsense/indexer Parse Markdown/MDX and build the index @docsense/runtime Browser/Node client that loads the JSON file docusaurus-plugin-docsense Wires indexing into Docusaurus and provides the SearchBar Most sites only install the plugin. The other packages are used underneath, or when you want a custom UI.

sections.title: Compared to hosted search
sections.content: Hosted search (for example Algolia DocSearch) Docsense --- --- External crawler or push API Index during your docs build Query hits a cloud service Query runs in the browser Freshness depends on crawl or sync jobs Freshness matches your last deploy Choose hosted search when you need a managed platform at large scale. Choose Docsense when you want search to stay inside your docs build and deploy. For the full open-source comparison (Docsense vs easyops, Orama, Pagefind, and DocSearch), see Compare open-source Docusaurus search.

documents.title: Indexing

sections.title: What gets indexed
sections.content: For each Markdown or MDX file, Docsense stores: - Title from frontmatter (title or sidebar label) or the first heading - Sections from headings (##, ###, and so on), including body text under each heading - Code blocks under those headings (kept for ranking) - Tags from tags or keywords in frontmatter when present - Page type , version , and language (from path, frontmatter, or plugin defaults)

sections.title: Page types
sections.content: Filters in the search modal use pageType. Docsense sets page type in this order: 1. Explicit pageType in frontmatter 2. Inferred from the URL path 3. Fallback to page or docs Path rules: Path contains Page type --- --- /how-to or /howto howto /concept concept /reference reference /tutorial tutorial /api or api-reference api /blog blog /docs (and none of the above) docs Example frontmatter:
code:
---
title: Install Docsense
pageType: howto
---

sections.title: What is stripped (and what MDX keeps)
sections.content: The indexer turns Markdown into plain text for search. It removes common markup noise and also: - Drops import / export lines and MDX comments - Keeps string values from textish JSX attributes (title, description, alt, aria-label, label, cta, and similar) Critical terms should still appear in headings or prose when possible. See MDX extraction and stemming.

sections.title: Where the index lives
sections.content: Default output: Change the relative path with the plugin indexPath option. The SearchBar loads it from your site root (for example /docsense/search-index.json).
code: static/docsense/search-index.json

documents.title: Ranking and typos

sections.title: Matching
sections.content: For each query word, Docsense looks for: 1. Exact match 2. Stem match (English Porter stem: installing ↔ install) 3. Prefix match (query is the start of a longer word) 4. Fuzzy match with a small edit distance Edit distance uses Damerau–Levenshtein (insert, delete, replace, and adjacent transpose). Short tokens allow fewer edits than longer tokens, so short words do not match unrelated words too easily. API-like tokens (paths, versions, identifiers with / # .) are not stemmed. See MDX extraction and stemming.

sections.title: Scoring
sections.content: Matches in different fields carry different weight. In order of importance: 1. Page title 2. Section title 3. Code 4. Breadcrumbs 5. Body text Docsense also boosts results when more of your query words match, and when the full query matches the page title.

sections.title: Pages vs sections
sections.content: Internally, Docsense can score section-level hits. The modal then keeps the best hit per page so you see a clean list of pages (default up to 8), not many rows from the same page.

sections.title: Tips for authors
sections.content: - Use clear, specific headings. Section titles are strong ranking signals. - Put important terms in the title or early headings when readers will search for them. - Prefer normal spelling in docs. Typo tolerance helps readers; it does not replace clear writing.

documents.title: Why Docsense

sections.title: What readers are actually trying to do
sections.content: A documentation visit usually ends in one of these outcomes: Outcome What success looks like --- --- Follow a procedure Open the canonical how-to and complete the steps Confirm a contract Land on the reference page for a field, error, or endpoint Recover from failure Reach the troubleshooting section that matches the symptom Share the answer Send a stable URL to a teammate, customer, or ticket Return later Bookmark or search again for the same page Ask AI can help with the first pass. It summarizes, suggests next steps, and reduces blank-page friction. It does not replace the need for a stable, authored page that your team maintains, versions, and links. Search is how readers (and your own support team) get back to that page on purpose.

sections.title: Why Ask AI does not retire documentation search
sections.content: Strong documentation sites often ship both an assistant and search because each one covers a failure mode the other does not.

sections.title: Readers often need the official page, not a paraphrase
sections.content: When someone needs the Install guide, the webhook signature reference, or the migration note for their version, success is opening that page and working from it. Search is built around that outcome: a short list of pages, section deep links, breadcrumbs, and filters that follow how the docs are organized. An assistant can explain the same topic well and still fail to put the required page in front of the reader.

sections.title: Authored docs are the system of record
sections.content: Your Markdown and MDX are reviewed, versioned, and deployed with the product. That corpus is the source of truth. Search makes that corpus navigable. An assistant reads from the corpus (or from a derived index) and produces a new answer each time. Even when retrieval is good, the reader experiences a generated response, not the maintained document. For API contracts, security steps, and breaking changes, teams usually want the maintained document in front of the reader.

sections.title: Predictability matters in support and compliance
sections.content: The same query in search should return the same short list of pages. Assistants vary. Phrasing, model updates, and conversation context change the answer. That flexibility is useful for exploration. It is costly when support macros, partner onboarding, or audit trails depend on a known page URL.

sections.title: Private and partner docs change the economics
sections.content: Ask AI introduces model access, retention policy, evaluation, and often a network call. Many Docusaurus sites are not fully public: partner portals, internal runbooks, staging docs, SSO-gated product docs. For those sites, the hard requirement is often: - Do not send the documentation corpus to a third-party crawler or model by default - Keep indexing inside the documentation build you already trust - Keep query behavior local to the site you already host Local documentation search is the layer that satisfies those constraints without asking you to stand up an assistant stack first.

sections.title: Assistants still depend on a findable docs corpus
sections.content: If titles, headings, and page structure are weak, both human search and retrieval-augmented assistants get worse. A maintained search index over your docs improves the corpus you already publish, whether or not you also ship chat.

sections.title: What was already hard before Ask AI
sections.content: Even before assistants were common, documentation search for Docusaurus forced awkward tradeoffs: Pressure What teams feel --- --- Hosted search Account, crawler or sync pipeline, procurement, and an external data boundary Freshness Docs deploy today; the index catches up later Local options Possible, but uneven on docs UX, ranking, filters, theming, or setup cost “Ship something” A search box that exists, but returns weak or opaque results Ask AI did not remove those pressures. In many programs it added a second surface while the underlying findability problem remained.

sections.title: What Docsense is for
sections.content: Docsense is the default local search layer for Docusaurus documentation sites that want to own findability without owning a search service. Concretely, it does four things that map to the problems above: 1. Indexes at build time with your docs, so the index updates when the site updates. 2. Ships a static JSON index with the site, so there is no Docsense query cloud and no crawler account for the core path. 3. Provides a documentation SearchBar with section results, page-type filters, typo tolerance, and theming. 4. Stays install-simple : add the plugin, rebuild, use search. It is not an Ask AI product. It is the findability layer you still need when you have an assistant, when you plan to add one, or when an assistant is the wrong first investment for private docs.

sections.title: When this matters most
sections.content: Choose a dedicated documentation search layer like Docsense when: - Readers must land on canonical pages, not only conversational answers - Docs change often enough that a stale index creates real support cost - Content is private, partner-gated, or otherwise sensitive to leave your boundary for indexing - You want open-source local search on Docusaurus with a complete SearchBar, not a hosted account as the default Prefer a hosted search platform or an assistant-first stack when your main requirement is managed operations, vendor Ask AI, or search far beyond a Docusaurus Markdown documentation tree. Compare open-source Docusaurus search covers those paths.

sections.title: Bottom line
sections.content: If your docs program only invests in Ask AI, readers can still struggle to open the maintained page, share a stable URL, or trust that today’s deploy is what search will show them tomorrow. Docsense covers that gap for Docusaurus: local indexing at build time, a static index you deploy with the site, and a SearchBar meant for documentation findability. You can add an assistant later. You should not postpone page search until you do.

It is the findability layer you still need when you have an assistant, when you plan to add one, or when an assistant is the wrong first investment for private docs. When this matters most Choose a dedicated documentation search layer like Docsense when: - Readers must land on canonical pages, not only conversational answers - Docs change often enough that a stale index creates real support cost - Content is private, partner-gated, or otherwise sensitive to leave your boundary for indexing - You want open-source local search on Docusaurus with a complete SearchBar, not a hosted account as the default Prefer a hosted search platform or an assistant-first stack when your main requirement is managed operations, vendor Ask AI, or search far beyond a Docusaurus Markdown documentation tree. Compare open-source Docusaurus search covers those paths. Bottom line If your docs program only invests in Ask AI, readers can still struggle to open the maintained page, share a stable URL, or trust that today’s deploy is what search will show them tomorrow. Docsense covers that gap for Docusaurus: local indexing at build time, a static index you deploy with the site, and a SearchBar meant for documentation findability. You can add an assistant later. You should not postpone page search until you do. documents.title: FAQ

sections.title: Does Docsense require an Algolia account?
sections.content: No. Docsense indexes your docs at build time and searches in the browser against a static JSON file. There is no Docsense cloud account and no crawler approval step.

sections.title: Where is the search index stored?
sections.content: By default the plugin writes: That file deploys with your site. You can change the path with the plugin indexPath option. See Indexing.
code: static/docsense/search-index.json

sections.title: Why does the Pages − control stop at 3?
sections.content: The SearchBar clamps the visible page count between 3 and 20 . At 3, the − button is disabled. At 20, the + button is disabled. The default starting value is 8 . See Use filters and page limits.

sections.title: Can readers filter by page type?
sections.content: Yes. When results include more than one page type, the modal shows chips such as How-to, Concept, and Reference. Types come from folder paths or from pageType in frontmatter.

sections.title: Does search work for private or internal docs?
sections.content: Yes, as long as readers can load your static site (and the index file). Docsense does not send document content to a Docsense server for indexing or querying.

sections.title: Does Docsense index MDX?
sections.content: Yes. The indexer reads Markdown and MDX, including many string attributes such as title and description. Put critical terms in headings or prose when possible. See MDX extraction and stemming.

sections.title: Will a typo still find the right page?
sections.content: Often yes. Docsense uses exact, prefix, and fuzzy matching, plus English stemming. Short tokens allow fewer edits than longer tokens. See Ranking and typos.

sections.title: How do I change the SearchBar label or colors?
sections.content: - Labels, shortcut, and empty-state copy: Customize the search bar - Colors and radius: Style the search UI

sections.title: Why does Docsense exist if Algolia and other search options already exist?
sections.content: Hosted and existing local options leave gaps around deploy freshness, private-docs data boundaries, and docs-native SearchBar UX. See Why Docsense.

sections.title: How does Docsense compare with easyops, Orama, Pagefind, and Algolia?
sections.content: See Compare open-source Docusaurus search.

sections.title: Is Ask AI included?
sections.content: Not in the current release. Optional Ask AI integration is on the feature roadmap.

documents.title: Highlight terms on the page

sections.title: What it is for
sections.content: Without highlights With highlights --- --- Reader lands on a long page and scans manually Matching words are marked in the article body Easy to lose the connection to the query Query intent stays visible for a moment after navigation

sections.title: How it works
sections.content: 1. The reader runs a query in the SearchBar. 2. On result click, Docsense stores the query in sessionStorage (short TTL). 3. After navigation, a client module finds the main article content, wraps matching terms in , and scrolls the first mark into view when the URL has no hash. :::note If the result URL includes a section hash (for example #install-the-plugin), the browser still scrolls to that heading. Highlights are applied in addition to the hash scroll. :::
code:
flowchart LR
  A[Search query] --> B[Click result]
  B --> C[Store query in sessionStorage]
  C --> D[Open destination page]
  D --> E[Mark matching terms]
  E --> F[Scroll to first mark]

sections.title: What gets marked
sections.content: Docsense tokenizes the query, then marks whole words on the page that either: - match a query token exactly (case-insensitive), or - share an English stem with a query token (so installing can mark Install) It never paints a stem fragment such as Instal inside a longer word. Short stop words are skipped. Code blocks, , and content are left alone so samples stay readable.

sections.title: Style the marks
sections.content: See Style the search UI for a full theme example.

sections.title: Privacy and limits
sections.content: - The pending query lives only in the reader’s sessionStorage and expires quickly. - Highlights run entirely in the browser. Nothing is sent to a Docsense server. - If storage is blocked, navigation still works; marks are simply skipped.

documents.title: MDX extraction and stemming

sections.title: What it is for
sections.content: Many Docusaurus pages mix Markdown with MDX components: A naive stripper that only removes tags would drop Install the plugin first. Docsense pulls textish attributes (such as title, description, alt, aria-label, label, cta) and keeps surrounding prose so those words stay searchable. It also drops import / export lines and MDX comments so they do not pollute the index.

sections.content: … Content Indexed? --- --- Markdown headings and prose Yes Fenced code bodies Yes (as code) String attributes like title="…" Yes Text only inside complex runtime components with no string props Often no. sections.content: Readers type different word forms than your docs use: Query Docs say Without stemming With stemming --- --- --- --- installing plugin Install the plugin May miss Matches streaming audio Stream live audio Weaker Stronger Docsense runs a compact Porter stemmer on English tokens during matching. Exact matches still score highest; stem matches score just below exact and above fuzzy typos.

documents.title: Features overview

sections.title: Search from the navbar
sections.content: Docsense registers a SearchBar in the Docusaurus navbar. Readers open it from the trigger control or with: - macOS: ⌘K - Windows and Linux: Ctrl+K You can change the trigger label, placeholder, shortcut, and empty-state copy. See Customize the search bar.

sections.title: Build-time indexing
sections.content: Docsense does not crawl your published site. On docusaurus start and docusaurus build, the plugin scans your Markdown and MDX, extracts searchable text (including many MDX string attributes), and writes static/docsense/search-index.json. The index deploys with the rest of your static assets, so search freshness matches the build you shipped.

sections.title: Section-level results
sections.content: Results can deep-link to a heading. Each hit includes breadcrumbs and a short snippet so readers can judge relevance before they click.

sections.title: Filters and page limits
sections.content: The modal can filter by page type (How-to, Concept, Reference, and related types inferred from paths or frontmatter). The default page limit is 8 . Readers change it with Pages − / + . The control stops at 3 on the low end and 20 on the high end; those buttons disable at the edges. See Use filters and page limits.

sections.title: Typo tolerance and stemming
sections.content: Queries use exact, prefix, and fuzzy matching, plus English stemming so forms such as installing and install connect. Details live in Ranking and typos and MDX extraction and stemming.

sections.title: Highlight on the destination page
sections.content: After a reader opens a result, Docsense can mark matching terms on the destination page so the jump from search to content stays oriented. See Highlight terms on the page.

sections.title: Custom look and feel
sections.content: Theme the SearchBar with CSS variables (colors, radius, modal chrome, and mark styles). This site’s deep green and gold theme is documented with a worked example in Style the search UI.

sections.title: Feature roadmap
sections.content: The following capabilities are planned. They are not available in the current release. Capability Direction --- --- Sharded indexes Split large indexes so the browser can load only the fragments a query needs. Intended for documentation sites whose single JSON index becomes too large to download up front. Broader language support Expand tokenization and stemming beyond the current English-first path, including CJK and additional locales. Optional Ask AI integration Support partner- or self-hosted answer experiences on top of the existing search index, without requiring a Docsense-hosted model service.

sections.title: Sharded indexes
sections.content: Today Docsense ships one static JSON index per site. That model is simple, inspectable, and a strong fit for typical documentation sets. Sharding is the roadmap path for very large corpora: a new index layout, a loader that fetches fragments on demand, and caching so repeat queries stay fast. Until that ships, prefer Docsense for sites where a single index download is acceptable. For multi-site HTML at extreme scale, Pagefind remains a common alternative. See Compare open-source Docusaurus search.

sections.title: Copy this config
sections.content: docusaurus.config.ts ```ts title="docusaurus.config.ts" plugins: [ [ 'docusaurus-plugin-docsense', , }, ], ], themeConfig: , }, },
code: Optional overrides under `themeConfig.docsense` (also used on this site):

## What each field does

| Field | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `placeholder` | `Search docs…` | Text inside the modal input |
| `triggerLabel` | `Search` | Navbar button label |
| `shortcut` | `mod+k` | Keyboard shortcut (`mod` is ⌘ on macOS and Ctrl elsewhere) |
| `showShortcutHint` | `true` | Show the shortcut key on the trigger |
| `modalAriaLabel` | `Search docs` | Accessible name for the modal |
| `emptyResultsLabel` | `No results` | Copy when a query has no hits |
| `debounceMs` | `120` | Wait time before running a query while typing |

## Change the default page count

`resultLimit` sets the starting number of pages in the modal (default **8**). Readers can still change it with **Pages − / +**. The UI clamps that control between **3** and **20**, and disables − or + at those edges so the count cannot go below 3 or above 20.
## Point at different docs folders

`docsRouteBasePath` must match how Docusaurus serves those pages so result links resolve correctly.

documents.title: Use filters and page limits

sections.title: Filter by page type
sections.content: After you type a query, Docsense shows chips such as All , How-to , or Concept when those types appear in the results. 1. Open search ( ⌘K / Ctrl+K ). 2. Enter a query. 3. Click a chip to keep only that page type. 4. Click All to clear the filter. If a chip no longer appears for a new query, Docsense falls back to All . Page types come from your folder paths or from pageType in frontmatter. See Indexing.

sections.title: Change how many pages are shown
sections.content: Next to the filters, use Pages − / + : - Default: 8 pages - Minimum: 3 (the − button disables at 3; the modal will not show fewer than three pages) - Maximum: 20 (the + button disables at 20) That floor of three is intentional. It keeps the result list usable and matches the clamp in the SearchBar UI. This limit counts pages , not every section under a page. Docsense keeps the best matching section for each page in the list.

sections.title: Author tip for better filters
sections.content: Group docs in clear folders: Those paths map to filter chips automatically. You can also set pageType in frontmatter when a file lives outside those folders.
code:
docs/
  concepts/
  how-to/

documents.body: The search modal includes two controls above the result list. Filter by page type After you type a query, Docsense shows chips such as All , How-to , or Concept when those types appear in the results. 1. Open search ( ⌘K / Ctrl+K ). 2. Enter a query. 3. Click a chip to keep only that page type. 4. Click All to clear the filter. If a chip no longer appears for a new query, Docsense falls back to All . Page types come from your folder paths or from pageType in frontmatter. See Indexing. Change how many pages are shown Next to the filters, use Pages − / + : - Default: 8 pages - Minimum: 3 (the − button disables at 3; the modal will not show fewer than three pages) - Maximum: 20 (the + button disables at 20) That floor of three is intentional. It keeps the result list usable and matches the clamp in the SearchBar UI. This limit counts pages , not every section under a page. Docsense keeps the best matching section for each page in the list. Author tip for better filters Group docs in clear folders: Those paths map to filter chips automatically. You can also set pageType in frontmatter when a file lives outside those folders. documents.title: What is Docsense?

sections.title: Who it is for
sections.content: Use Docsense if you want to: - Add search to a Docusaurus site without a hosted search product - Keep the search index in sync with every docs deploy - Search private or internal docs without sending content to a third-party crawler - Own and inspect the index file yourself

Readers change the count with − / +. The − control stops at 3 (it will not go lower). The + control stops at 20 . Typo tolerance Finds results even when a query has small spelling mistakes Custom labels and CSS Change copy, shortcut, and colors to match your site

sections.title: How it fits together
sections.content: 1. You add the docusaurus-plugin-docsense plugin. 2. On each build, Docsense reads your docs and writes static/docsense/search-index.json. 3. Readers open search in the browser. Queries run locally against that JSON file.

sections.title: Top-level options
sections.content: Option Type Default Description --- --- --- --- docsDirs string[] ['docs'] Folders to scan, relative to the site root docsRouteBasePath string '/docs' URL prefix used when building result links indexPath string 'docsense/search-index.json' Output path under static/ defaultVersion string 'current' Default version facet on documents defaultLanguage string 'en' Default language facet on documents resultLimit number 8 Initial page count in the modal searchBar object see below Labels and modal behavior

sections.title: searchBar options
sections.content: Option Type Default Description --- --- --- --- placeholder string 'Search docs…' Modal input placeholder triggerLabel string 'Search' Navbar button label shortcut string 'mod+k' Keyboard shortcut showShortcutHint boolean true Show shortcut on the trigger modalAriaLabel string 'Search docs' aria-label for the modal emptyResultsLabel string 'No results' Empty-state message debounceMs number 120 Query debounce in milliseconds

sections.title: Example
code:
[
  'docusaurus-plugin-docsense',
  {
    docsDirs: ['docs'],
    docsRouteBasePath: '/docs',
    indexPath: 'docsense/search-index.json',
    defaultVersion: 'current',
    defaultLanguage: 'en',
    resultLimit: 8,
    searchBar: {
      placeholder: 'Search the docs…',
      triggerLabel: 'Search docs',
      shortcut: 'mod+k',
      showShortcutHint: true,
      modalAriaLabel: 'Search docs',
      emptyResultsLabel: 'No results',
      debounceMs: 120,
    },
  },
]

sections.title: Report a bug or request a feature
sections.content: Open an issue on GitHub: github.com/meharshit/docsense/issues Include: - Docsense / plugin version (or git commit) - Docusaurus version - Steps to reproduce - Expected result and actual result - Relevant config snippets (docusaurus.config plugin options, not secrets)

sections.title: Ask a question
sections.content: Use GitHub Issues for product questions that may help other readers, or start a discussion on the repository if Discussions are enabled for the project. Before you open a new thread, check: - FAQ - Install Docsense - Plugin options

sections.title: Security
sections.content: If you believe you found a security issue in Docsense, do not file a public issue with exploit details. Contact the maintainer through GitHub and mark the report as security-sensitive when the repository supports that workflow.
